Stone and Courses

A wall or cliff built from a footprint and filled with courses of stone. Every stone is the rock of the Weathered Stone page, and one union joins them for the printability gate. Four panels hold every control: the region, the courses that fill it, each stone’s own region, and the rock in it.

1 · The editor

Pick a wall, then change any control: the model rebuilds and the gate judges it. The cells show at once and each stone replaces its cell as it is finished; one union (955 ms for a 1×1, preset L, draft) joins the meshes for the gate. Over 114 builds (19 presets, both systems, 3 seeds each, draft) the gate passes 27 as the page’s dot judges it, and 85 when the bridge faces (painted blue) are counted apart. Hover a control to see what it does and to jump to its step. Scale: 35 mm squares are DungeonBlocks, 25.4 mm are OpenLOCK. Rejected explorations and old measurements are in the decisions log.

2 · The algorithm, step by step

The wall is built in thirteen steps, in four parts that are the editor’s four panels: the region, the courses that fill it, each stone’s own region, and the rock in it. Each step says what it does in one sentence, shows the photograph it aims at, explains how it works, draws the mechanism, and lists the controls that drive it. Click or tap a reference photograph to flip it between painted and unpainted: the unpainted one shows the geometry.

Step 0 The viewer

The viewer shows what the build makes, one step at a time, and each control changes one word.

Goal

Show the build one step at a time, so that every word can be tried and its effect seen.

The editor at the top of the page is the algorithm made visible. The Level strip stops the build after any step; opening a panel moves it to the step that shows that panel. The icons on the canvas change what you look at: the model in 3D, the plan from above, the elevation from the front, or the costs. The grey, red and green dot at the top right is the printability gate (step 10).

Controls are inputs only. Everything the build reports is a view. Hover a control, or tap its label on a phone, to read what it does and jump to the step that explains it.

Takes in
a preset: a set of dial values, one per word, and a seed
Hands on
a built wall (a list of convex solids), its gate verdict and its costs

1 Region

Where the cliff stands: its footprint, top line and faces.

Steps 1, 3a. Panel 1 in the editor.

Step 1 (L0) The footprint and the crest

The wall stands inside a box: the footprint, kept 0.6 mm inside the tile edge, and the crest above it.

The tile is a 35 mm square (DungeonBlocks) or 25.4 mm (OpenLOCK); a wall of Run 2x1 is two squares long. The footprint is the rectangle left after the margin, from the preset’s front back by region depth; a preset with a wing makes it an L, so a corner can be built. The crest is the height of the top along the wall. It is drawn by the graded rule: a smooth wobble with crest bumps per square, ranked, and each rank mapped through the crest weighting into the band between the two ends of top, so the crest uses its whole band at every seed. The dirt is 3.4 mm thick and the crest is measured above it.

Why. Everything later is measured against this box, and the margin is what lets two tiles stand side by side.

Step 3a (L2) The face band

A course’s face stands between today’s face and one face depth behind it, drawn by the graded rule, on every free face that is switched on.

One rule draws the crest, a course’s face and a stone’s outline. Make a smooth wobble along the line, with bumps for how many wobbles; rank it; map each rank through the weighting’s quantile to a place t in the gap; a point’s distance is inner plus gap times t. The weighting says how far, bumps says how many, so the line has exactly the weighting’s mix of distances and only where they fall changes. Here the inner line is the footprint’s straight face, the gap is face depth, and each course draws its own line from its own keyed seed (a line for each course and each face). The cells stay convex; each stone is cut to its course’s edge when its cell is handed to the rock, and joints never move. Face depth 0 is the straight face, exactly.

Which faces. A free face is a side of the footprint that stands in the air: front, back, left or right. A seam (the wall going on into the next tile, or the hill behind it) is never free. The Free faces group in the Region panel has one switch each for front, back and sides, and they govern this band, recess (step 5a) and the lip together: front is on and the others off unless you turn them on. Each effect is written once, in the face’s own frame (along the face, and out of the wall), so the front is the plain case of the general rule and a corner where two faces are on is cut by both. Back acts only on a free-standing footprint (a wall’s back is a seam, or, with Wall on, the mirrored front); sides act on a free-standing footprint and on the step of an L, and the left and right sides each draw their own line from the one switch. The picture shows preset C with the front only, then with all three on.

stay behind sets a course never in front of the one under it: node by node the edge is the larger of the course’s own line and the one below, so the band itself adds no overhang (a head joint opened by a stone recessed in step 5a can). A lip course stands out on purpose and is left alone. With stay behind off, each course draws its own line and may overhang.

Why. The band gives a face variety without ledges; the running maximum is the price, so the face of a tall wall drifts toward the outer line. The foot band of step 10 is a different thing.

2 Courses

How the region is filled: courses of stones.

Steps 2, 3, 4, 5, 5a, 6, 7. Panel 2 in the editor.

Step 2 (L1) The row planes

Every row boundary is drawn for the whole wall before a single stone exists.

Row heights are drawn between the two ends of height (with height skew) until they reach the highest crest, then scaled to fit it exactly. Each boundary between two rows is a plane through the whole wall: lean (side to side, the slope along the wall) and tilt (front to back, the slope into it) turn it, each drawn from its own range in degrees across the planes up the wall by one weighting, so the rows run from a low angle to a high one (a range may be negative); wave adds two waves and a little noise on top. The ground plane stays flat. No two planes may come closer than 0.6 of a row: the ranges are held to the angles that keep that true, before anything is drawn, and the card says when a range was limited and to what. A plane is laid on a grid of flat triangles, so every stone that stands on one triangle shares exactly that plane. The stone sites sit on a grid set by the middle of width; regularity decides how far they are shaken from it; from one row to the next, bond is the chance a site moves and shift is how far.

Why. A stone that follows a plane has a flat bed exactly on the top below it, which is what keeps stacked stones from hanging in air.

Step 3 (L2) Subdividing a row

A row is cut into stones by dividing the area the rows below left it: each site owns the cell closer to it than to any other.

The area a row may fill is the footprint; a lip row moves out instead (the setback is each stone’s, step 5a). Each site owns the part of that area nearer to it than to any other site, cut off exactly at the area’s edge. An L is first cut into convex parts. Neighbouring cells overlap by 0.15 mm at each joint, so the union has no coincident faces. A stone that carries on up through the row keeps its footprint (step 4): its site stays as a ghost, so the cells round it stay whole. A cell is one Voronoi cell, not cut along the stones under it (a lip row is the exception); what it stands on is the rock’s business (step 8). A cell that is too small or too thin to hold the rock is not made, a cell with too little support is dropped, and so is one that the crest leaves too short, so the upper courses form a stepped mound under the crest.

Why. Cells that fill the area exactly give joints only where two stones meet.

Step 4 (L2) Rise: a stone carries on

A stone rolls, again and again, to carry on up through the next row.

Every stone starts in one row. It rolls against rise: on success it carries on into the next row and rolls again, stopping at the first failure or at the top. At 0 every stone is one row; near 1 stones run all the way up. A stone that rises keeps its footprint in the rows above: the other cells of those rows end on the footprint's own edge, never inside it (each cell the footprint reaches is cut by the one edge line that loses it least, so cells and the tall stone share an edge and no area), and its top is the top plane of the last row it reaches. The rock may cut a stone's edges and corners, but never takes a whole bed (the ground or the stone it stands on) or a top: a stone always stands on what it stands on. A stone on a lip row never rises.

Why. A tall stone is one convex piece, so it is never a bridge, and its neighbours cannot overlap it; the stones above it rest on the stones below as before.

Step 5 (L2) Span: neighbours join

Neighbours that stand between the same two planes roll to become one stone.

After the stones have risen, two neighbours may join if they start on the same row and end on the same row. Each such pair rolls against span. A pair that joins is one stone: the edge between them is no joint and no free face, and the rock is built once for the whole group, from the union of their cells, with a crack where they met that no cut or wear takes. The group shares one top (the highest of its cells); each cell keeps the bed it stands on. At 0 every pair stays apart; at 1 every pair that can join does, and a course between two lips can be one long stone.

Why. A wide stone is one rock, as a tall stone (rise) is: there is no groove across it and wear, grain and cuts run over the whole of it. It is the same by construction in both directions; the gate judges the result.

Step 5a (L2) Recess: each stone stands back

After the stones are made, carried up and joined, each stone with a free edge on a face that is switched on (Free faces) is set back by an amount of its own on that face.

The amount is drawn from the range of recess by the graded rule, along the course: the stones are ranked by a smooth wobble along the face (recess bumps per square, the same unit as the face band), a line for each face that is on (the front’s draw is the legacy one; each other face draws its own), and each rank is mapped through the recess weighting into the range. It is the one graded rule that also draws the crest, the face band and the stone outline; four callers, one function. A stone that has been joined (step 5) counts once and moves as one. A stone’s free edges on a face move back by that face’s amount: its cell is cut by a plane parallel to each, so a stone at a corner is set back on both faces. Seams are never set back. A head joint that this opens, where a neighbour now stands further back, becomes a free face; gaps between stones are fine. A lip row keeps its own rule, and recess does not apply to it.

The face band (step 3a) and recess are two things. The band is a line: a cut across the stones of a course. Recess is a stone property: whole stones stepped back. Both stand behind the straight face, so a stone is cut by the band first and recessed after, and where they differ the further back wins.

There is no offset for the whole row and nothing accumulates from one course to the next, so there is no stay behind for the row, but a stone is never recessed less than the stones under it on the same face; a wall that should lean gets its lean from the region’s face, not from recess. A free face opened by a head joint can overhang a little, which the gate counts like any other. A stone above stands on the tops of the stones below as before (step 8); one that loses its support is dropped.

Why. A row set back by one constant amount is a smooth ledge; a stone recessed by its own amount gives the broken front of real rock, and a joined stone moving as one stays a single stone.

Step 6 (L2) Building a stone

Each stone becomes a solid between the plane under it and the plane over it.

A cell is a polygon and the stone is its prism, from the bed to the top. The bed is the top of whatever is under it; the top is the bed plus the row’s height, or the sum of the rows it rises through. wander changes each stone’s height at random by up to its share of the row; at 0 every stone ends on its plane. Every stone gets its top when it is built: its row’s top plane intersected with the cliff’s envelope, the footprint carried up to the crest, so no stone rises above the crest and none is cut afterwards. A stone the crest leaves under the minimum stone height (4 mm at the 35 mm square) is not built. On tilted or waved planes a stone that stands on several facets is one piece for each facet, each cut by that facet’s own plane. Wall on mirrors the wall onto the back.

The prism is the stone’s region: its area carried up from its bed to its top. Step 8 hands that area and top to the rock, which works inside it as the Weathered Stone page works inside a box. The editor draws the cells as soon as they are made, then each stone as its rock arrives.

Why. A bed that is exactly the stone below leaves no flat ceiling, which the gate would count as overhang. There is no seal: stones meet exactly at their planes.

Step 7 (L3) Joints

It decides which faces of a stone are joints and which neighbours are one stone; it cuts nothing.

Step 3 marked every edge of every cell: a joint is shared with a neighbour, a free edge is open to the air, and an edge between cells that step 5 merged is joined. This step reads those marks and hands them on. The neighbours touch behind the face, each overlapping the next by 0.15 mm in plan. The V in a finished wall is not carved here: it is the groove the rock’s wear opens in step 8 where a surface meets a joint face. A joint face is held by the neighbour, so the rock never cuts it and wear rounds only its edge.

Why. Change which faces are joints and the weathering follows; nothing is written twice.

3 Rock region

Each stone's own region: its outline, what it bears on, its top.

Steps 7a, 9. Panel 3 in the editor.

Step 7a (L4) The stone outline

Each stone’s footprint lies between a core and its cell, drawn by the same graded rule round a circle; joints never move.

The same rule as step 3a. Points are placed round the stone, each with a wobble value that is a smooth function of its angle with bumps whole bumps round it. The values are ranked, mapped through the weighting’s quantile, and each point goes to core plus (cell minus core) times (one minus strength times (one minus t)) along its ray from the stone’s centre: t of one is the cell, zero the core. Strength 0 hands on the cell exactly. Only free edges move; a joint keeps its end points and the outline eases back to the cell before one, so two neighbours meet at the same corner. The outline can be non-convex, so it is split into convex parts, which the rock takes; the edge two parts share is a crack inside the stone.

A stone is cut to what holds it: its area is intersected, in plan, with the final areas of the stones it rests on, course by course from the ground up, so a bed is always over material.

Why. The stone is no longer the Voronoi polygon with flat faces. Only free edges move, so a stone in the middle of a wall (all joints) does not change; a lower strength, fewer bumps or a larger core is calmer.

Step 9 (L2 to L4) Fitting to what is below

Where a stone stands over a stone that has been cut back, its bed is chamfered so that nothing hangs in air.

This is not a step of its own: it runs inside steps 3 to 8. Beds settle: a stone’s bed is the highest top of the stones under it, and they are raised to match until none moves. At each free edge the stone looks at the stones under it. If their top stops short of its edge, the edge is chamfered, steeper than the overhang limit, so the flat underside never starts in front of where the stone below stops. Where the stone below stops further back than the chamfer can reach and the bed would stay large enough, the edge is cut back vertically instead. Where a stone below has no other top beyond its outline, the bed is chamfered from that outline, and a lip stone is chamfered from each supporting stone’s outline. On a tilted bed the chamfers tilt with it. The rock does the same at the edges of a part it adds (the joint’s lower mouth, 0.72 mm deep).

Why. These rules are why a wall of stacked stones passes the gate at all. When a chamfer cannot make an edge safe nothing is done and the gate reports it; the walls marked “refuses” in the Preset list show what a switched-off rule costs.

4 Rock

What is done to each stone inside its region.

Steps 8, 10. Panel 4 in the editor.

Step 8 (L4) The rock

Every stone becomes the rock: its cell, weathered by six stages, each of which does nothing at 0.

Each stone’s cell is handed to the rock with the rock’s settings (the six stages of Weathered Stone, each with a strength, zero meaning off) and a seed; the rock hands back the stone’s surface as a closed mesh. It is the same code as the Weathered Stone page, one copy. The region it takes is an area and a top: the stone’s outline in plan, a bed under it and a top over it, each a plane. A face is held when something outside the stone holds it (the seat, or a joint); a held face is never rounded when it leans down, never chipped, and grain and pockets fade out on any face that leans down.

The cuts stage has three limits, preserve top, preserve sides and preserve bottom: how much of the stone, measured in from that face, no cut may reach. A bed carries bear, the convex hull of the cut tops of the stones below, intersected with the stone’s area: a hull is convex, so it is one polygon, and the cuts bring the bed inside it. A gap inside the hull is bridged; the bridge’s underside is flat and faces down, so the gate counts it, and the viewer paints it blue. A stone with nothing worth standing on is not built. Quality sets the sampling: draft or fine.

Why. The groove between two stones is the rock’s wear, opening where a surface meets a face a neighbour holds, so the wall has no second way to bevel, facet, tilt or chip a stone.

Step 10 (L5) The union and the gate

The pieces are joined into one body, and the gate checks that it can print.

Every convex piece is turned into its hull, and the hulls, the core behind the wall and the ground plate are united in one operation (Manifold). Then the gate reads the result. Watertight: the manifold’s status must be NoError. One body: only one piece with any volume. Overhang: the area of down-facing faces leaning more than 65 degrees must be at most a thousandth of the downward area, and the area between 55 and 65 degrees at most another thousandth; the bed on the ground is not counted. The editor also shows the printer’s line (0.45 mm) and layer (0.2 mm) in the Lines view and which faces are bridges; these are shown beside the verdict, not part of it.

Why. Nothing is culled and no threshold is ever changed to pass: a wall that fails is shown as failing.

4 · Printing

A printer lays 0.45 mm lines in 0.2 mm layers. A face that leans out more than 55 degrees is orange; more than 65 is red. The gate allows a thousandth of the downward area in each band. OpenLOCK (25.4 mm) prints every length at 0.7257 of its DungeonBlocks value, but the 0.45 mm line does not shrink.

Every printing rule is made by construction in one step, so most of what the gate would refuse is never built. What still fails is listed in Where the model breaks.

RuleStepWhat it guarantees
Set back first3, subdividing a rowa stone is never wider than what it stands on, except where step 9 chamfers it
A bed is the top below it6, building a stoneno flat ceiling between two stones (no seal: stones meet exactly)
The rock stays off held faces8, the rocka cut never touches a held top or bed, a held bed is not rounded, a chip never sits on its edge, and grain and pockets fade out on a face that leans down: nothing the rock does makes a stone hang further
Chamfered beds9, fitting to what is belowa bed over a cut-back edge is chamfered inside the overhang limit, before the rock sees the cell
The gate11, the union and the gatewatertight, one body, overhang within budget, or the build is refused

The editor’s Lines view shows the slice a slicer would cut at any height, and the section through the wall; parts thinner than one line are marked. These are shown, not part of the gate’s verdict.

What fails, and why

  • A groove has a roof. Wear opens a groove along every joint, and the stone above is a flat ceiling over it. The rock keeps a held bed sharp, but a chip is a cut with its own roof: chips and chunks are off in every wall because they fail the gate.
  • Cells the rock cannot save. The spires, the lips, the tilted rows and the courses of D, J and R fail with every stage at 0 or nearly: their cells already hang. The rock is held to no cuts on them.
  • Tilted and waved rows. Every piece of every stone has its bed on a different facet, so thin slivers appear everywhere. Row planes draw correctly and blocks follow them; most walls with dip or wave do not pass.
  • No seal. Stones meet exactly at their planes. Where two outlines differ by a hair, the union leaves thin down-facing slivers that count as overhang.
  • Convex cells. A stone with a hole, or a ring, is not reachable. A lip stone never rises, so a tall lip is not reachable.
  • Planes cannot be named. They are drawn at random; a document cannot give a wall a known rake or a step in its rows.
  • Photographs not yet reached. No wall reproduces the fine surface of the references: cracks, lichen, staining.

The Preset list marks the two walls meant to be refused (thin courses; wear and chips turned up); the sweep checks that the gate refuses them.

6 · The language

These are the words an author writes, each with one meaning. The editor’s controls, its pop-ups and the lists of controls in each step are all read from one table; this table is read from it too. A word the tile language already has is marked tile; the others are words of this page and are not yet in the tile language.

Design check

  • Words. The registry’s own words are reused (top, width, height, bond, seed). The registry’s depth means the gap between stones, so the cliff’s depth is region depth and the face band’s is face depth. The wall’s dip leans the row planes; the rock’s strata dip is not a wall word, because each stone takes its bed’s lean. A stone’s weathering is the rock’s six stages, one word each; the wall has no second way to bevel, facet, tilt or chip a stone.
  • Kinds. A control is a number, a range, a choice or a group (a stage, a weighting). A preset is a state of those controls, not a kind. A row plane is data of the build, not a kind a document can name, pass or override.
  • Kernel. Everything reduces to a partition per row, a roll per stone from one seeded stream, a prism cut by two planes, the rock, and one graded rule that draws the crest, a course’s front and a stone’s outline.
  • Second paths, left visible. Two rules share a range: the skew of width and height (a power law) and the weighting of the crest, front and outline. A column of stacked cells (bond near 0) and a risen stone differ only by the groove the rock’s wear opens. Wander and plane variation both vary heights.
  • Holes. Rise and span on sloped planes; a lip stone that rises; naming the row planes.

7 · The plan

The Rust engine builds a cliff tile today as one dense mesh of grain: 0.54 to 3.2 million triangles, a 2×2 corner at 7.3 GB resident (the library baseline of 15 Nov 2026, in docs/standards/performance.html; not measured here). This model builds a 1×1 tile from 6 to 94 stones, each a few convex pieces. It goes into the engine in this order; each stage has a small torture tile and the check that gates it.

  1. Footprint and crest, then the row planes. Torture tile: a J corner with dip on. Check: planes never closer than a share of a row.
  2. The partition. Torture tile: an L footprint. Check: the cells cover all of course 0.
  3. Rise and span. Torture tile: preset T. Check: no cell reaches past its supports; no loose body.
  4. Prisms between planes, then joints. Torture tile: preset S. Check: every bed is exactly the top below it.
  5. The rock, then the graded outline and front. Torture tiles: forms L (lip) and E (ledges). Check: overhang budget.
  6. The union and the gate. Check: every shipped wall passes in every seed; today 85 of 114 builds pass with bridges counted apart.

Appendix · How the photographs were measured

The reference panels (L, B, E, M, G, O, F, A, N and their crops) were measured against the 28 mm figure that stands in each (about 295 px tall in a 800 px panel); distances farther from the camera than the figure read short. Every measurement carries about ±25%. Row heights, stone widths, joint widths and facet sizes in each step are read this way and set that step’s defaults.
